title: Em Causal Response And Radiation Prerequisites

items.title: Causal convolution response, transfer function and dispersion relations
items.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#D1-D2 (compact and W^{1,1} integrable causal branches), assembled with the passivity quadratic form
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the smooth Riemann/Lebesgue comparison route below; in clause (c), also assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) inherited from the AC supplier. Let $d\ge1$. All kernels below are real $d\times d$ matrix kernels and all histories are $\mathbb R^d$-valued; conditions on matrices are read entrywise, and $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ means entrywise Lebesgue integrability on $(0,\infty)$.

(a) (Causal convolution.) Let $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and continuous. Then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the integral $P(t):=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely, $$|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d\Bigl(\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|E_k(s)|\Bigr)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds\qquad(j=1,\dots,d),$$ the response $P$ is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal: if $E_1,E_2$ are bounded continuous and coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$, then their responses coincide on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

(b) (Compact branch.) If $K\in C_c^\infty((0,\infty);\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ (smooth, with compact support contained in the open half-line), then the transfer function $$\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for every real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$. For any $b>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$, the full entire-plane bound is $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}\|K_{jk}\prime\prime\|_1|z|^{-2}$ for every $z\ne0$. Its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations $$\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,\qquad \operatorname{Im}\chi_{jk}(\omega)=-\frac1\pi\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}\chi_{jk}(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi$$ for every real $\omega$.

(c) (Integrable branch.) If instead $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is locally absolutely continuous entrywise in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]] on every compact subinterval of $[0,\infty)$, with $K\prime$ its almost-everywhere derivative with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and $s\mapsto sK(s)$ in $L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$, then $\chi(z):=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on the open upper half-plane $\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the same pair of dispersion relations for every real $\omega$, and is bounded on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ by $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le|K_{jk}(0)|+\|K_{jk}'\|_{L^1(0,\infty)}$ for $|z|\ge1$; for an instantaneous real response matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ define $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}:=\chi_\infty+\chi$ and apply the relations to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$.

(d) (Monochromatic work and passivity.) Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^d$, and let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be a real parameter (a response normalization; the equivalence below is independent of its value). Put $E(t):=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{-i\omega t})$ and $P(t):=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, real parts taken componentwise and $\chi(\omega)$ acting by matrix multiplication. Then, with $T:=2\pi/\omega$ and the Euclidean dot product on $\mathbb R^d$, $$\frac1T\int_0^T E(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),\qquad e^*\chi(\omega)e:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\overline{e_j}\,\chi_{jk}(\omega)\,e_k,$$ and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$ if and only if the Hermitian dissipative part $M(\omega):=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e\in\mathbb C^d$.
items.strategy:
Proof technique: direct, branch by branch; clausal tags below indicate the cited tools.

(a) For each $j$ and $t$, absolute convergence and the displayed bound follow from $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$, the triangle inequality for integrals and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral over the measurable set $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]). Linearity in $E$ is linearity of the integral. Continuity in $t$: if $t_n\to t$ then $K_{jk}(s)E_k(t_n-s)\to K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)$ for every $s$ with the integrable dominating function $(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}|$, so dominated convergence gives $P(t_n)\to P(t)$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Causality: for $t\le t_0$ and every $s\ge0$ the argument $t-s$ lies in $(-\infty,t_0]$, so replacing $E$ by a history agreeing with it there changes no integrand value and hence no integral.

(b) Holomorphy is obtained from the real-parameter differentiation theorem rather than by differentiating in the complex variable directly. Writing $z=x+iy$, the integrand $K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}=K_{jk}(s)e^{ixs}e^{-ys}$ has continuous partials in $x$ and $y$; because $K_{jk}$ has compact support, on every compact set of parameters $(x,y)$ the partials are dominated by a fixed multiple of $|K_{jk}|(1+|s|)$, an integrable function, so [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]] applied in the two real parameters gives the continuous partials $\partial_x\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty isK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ and $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=\int_0^\infty(-s)K_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). These satisfy $\partial_y\chi_{jk}=-\int sK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\int isK_{jk}e^{izs}=i\,\partial_x\chi_{jk}$, the Cauchy--Riemann equations for the pair $(\partial_x\chi_{jk},\partial_y\chi_{jk})$ with the identification $f=u+iv$; since the partials exist on a neighbourhood and are continuous, [[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]] makes $\chi_{jk}$ holomorphic, and because the same argument is available at every $z\in\mathbb C$, each entry is entire ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). Iterating gives $\chi_{jk}^{(k)}(z)=\int_0^\infty(is)^kK_{jk}(s)e^{izs}\,ds$. For the reality identity at real $\omega$: conjugation is an isometry and a real-field automorphism of $\mathbb C$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and the series defining the complex exponential converges everywhere ([[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]); conjugating the partial sums termwise and passing to the limit along the isometry gives $\overline{e^{i\omega s}}=e^{-i\omega s}$, so conjugating the defining integral of $\chi_{jk}$ and using that $K_{jk}$ is real gives $\overline{\chi_{jk}(\omega)}=\int_0^\infty K_{jk}(s)e^{-i\omega s}\,ds=\chi_{jk}(-\omega)$ ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). On $[0,b]$, apply [[thm-integration-by-parts]] twice to the real and imaginary parts of the smooth exponential and real smooth kernel (first $K$, then $K\prime$). All derivatives are continuous and Riemann integrable; [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]] transfers each compact-interval identity to the Lebesgue integrals. With vanishing endpoint values because $K$ vanishes near $0$ and beyond $b$, these identities give $\chi_{jk}(z)=-z^{-2}\int_0^\infty K_{jk}''(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ for $z\ne0$, hence the stated upper-half-plane $|z|^{-2}$ bound; for arbitrary complex $z$, $|e^{izs}|\le e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ on the support gives the full entire-plane bound. For the dispersion relations fix real $\omega$ and form a contour consisting of the interval $[-R,R]$ indented above $\omega$ on a clockwise semicircle of radius $\delta$, closed by the large semicircle of radius $R$ in the upper half-plane; on the indented domain the integrand $\chi_{jk}(z)/(z-\omega)$ is holomorphic, so Cauchy's theorem for null-homotopic loops gives vanishing total integral ([[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]]). The large arc contributes at most $\pi R\sup_{|z|=R,\operatorname{Im}z\ge0}|\chi_{jk}|/(R-|\omega|)\to0$ by the $|z|^{-2}$ bound. The small arc contributes $-i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)+o(1)$ as $\delta\to0$, by continuity of $\chi_{jk}$ on the closed upper half-plane, which follows from dominated convergence as in (a) ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). The remaining real integral converges to its principal value: near $\omega$ subtract the constant $\chi_{jk}(\omega)$ so that the divided difference $[\chi_{jk}(\xi)-\chi_{jk}(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded, and at infinity use the $|z|^{-2}$ decay. Letting $\delta\to0$, $R\to\infty$ gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}\chi_{jk}(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi\chi_{jk}(\omega)$; separating real and imaginary parts yields the displayed pair because $i(a+ib)=-b+ia$.

(c) This is precisely the content of the cited integrable-causal-dispersion lemma: that item proves, under exactly these hypotheses, the holomorphy on the upper half-plane ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]), the closed-half-plane bound, the boundary regularity and the two principal-value formulas, and records the instantaneous-response subtraction ([[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]). The present theorem assembles the response, its transfer function and the passivity relation around that lemma; its explicit AC definition and Lebesgue FTC/integration-by-parts route apply entrywise under the inherited Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; its boundary contour uses vertical shifts before passing to the real boundary.

(d) The period-average of a product of real parts of complex exponentials is supplied by [[lem-em-period-average]], which states exactly $\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})dt=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(a\cdot\overline d)$; applying it with $a=e$ and $d=(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e$ (the derivative of $t\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e\,e^{-i\omega t})$, computed with the chain rule) gives $$\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(e\cdot\overline{(-i\omega)\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e}\Bigr)=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\bigl(e^*\chi(\omega)e\bigr),$$ using $e\cdot\overline{\chi(\omega)e}=\overline{e^*\chi(\omega)e}$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-iz)=\operatorname{Im}z$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]). Finally $e^*M(\omega)e=(e^*\chi(\omega)e-e^*\chi(\omega)^*e)/(2i)=\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$ because $M(\omega)$ is the Hermitian dissipative part of $\chi(\omega)$, so nonnegativity of the displayed average for every $e$ is exactly the stated quadratic-form condition. The logical independence of causality and this positivity (the design's 'no sign of dissipation follows merely from causality') is exhibited on the companion example page by a kernel satisfying (c) whose quadratic form is strictly negative.

items.title: Uniform far-zone asymptotics and retarded-time flux limit for compact conserved smooth sources
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the declared polar/surface and change-of-variables suppliers. Let $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$ and $t_0<T$ be constants, let $\rho\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ and $\mathbf J\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R;\mathbb R^3)$ satisfy (H1) $\rho(y,v)=\mathbf J(y,v)=0$ whenever $|y|>a$ or $v\notin[t_0,T]$, and (H2) $\partial_v\rho+\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Here and below $B_a:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:|y|<a\}$ and $\overline B_a:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:|y|\le a\}$ are the open and closed Euclidean balls of radius $a$ about the origin, and $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$ is the unit sphere. On the open exterior $U:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|>a\}$ define the retarded scalar and vector potentials $$\varphi(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0c^2}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad \mathbf A(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\mathbf J(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,$$ and the fields $\mathbf E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$, $\mathbf B:=\nabla\times\mathbf A$, where $\nabla f=(\partial_1f,\partial_2f,\partial_3f)$, $\operatorname{div}F=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_jF_j$ and $\nabla\times F=(\partial_2F_3-\partial_3F_2,\partial_3F_1-\partial_1F_3,\partial_1F_2-\partial_2F_1)$ are the spatial operators of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. The fields are defined on $U\times\mathbb R$ using these ordinary derivatives; the conclusions below use $r:=|x|\ge2a$. Every displayed spatial integrand is evaluated on $\overline B_a$ and extended by zero outside it, including at $y=x$, so no quotient $0/0$ is used. All vector-valued integrals are componentwise scalar Lebesgue integrals.

(a) (Fields as retarded integrals.) On the open set $\{|x|>2a\}$ the potentials $\varphi,\mathbf A$ are of class $C^\infty$ in $(x,t)$, and there $$\mathbf E(x,t)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf N}{R^2}c^2\rho\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)+\frac{c\,\mathbf N}{R}\rho_t\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)-\frac{\mathbf J_t\bigl(y,t-\tfrac Rc\bigr)}{R}\Bigr]dy,\qquad \mathbf B(x,t)=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\mathbf N\times\Bigl[\frac{\mathbf J(y,t-\frac Rc)}{R^2}+\frac{\mathbf J_t(y,t-\frac Rc)}{cR}\Bigr]dy,$$ where $R:=|x-y|$, $\mathbf N:=(x-y)/R$, and $\rho_t,\mathbf J_t$ are the partial derivatives in the second variable. Moreover, on $\{|x|\ge2a\}\times[t_0,T]$, $\varphi$ and each component of $\mathbf A$ coincide with the corresponding solution constructed in the wave Cauchy problem of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] for zero Cauchy data at $t_0$ and scalar source $h=\mu_0c^2\rho$, respectively $h=\mu_0 J_k$.

(b) (Uniform far-zone expansion.) For $n\in S^2$ and $u\in[t_0,T]$ put $\mathbf I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ and $\mathbf V(n,u):=\partial_u\mathbf I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$. Then $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy=\frac1c\,n\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$, and there are constants $\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$, depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and on the suprema of $|\rho|,|\rho_t|,|\rho_{tt}|,|\mathbf J|,|\mathbf J_t|,|\mathbf J_{tt}|$ on $\overline B_a\times[t_0,T]$, such that for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$ and $r\ge2a$, with $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathbf V(n,u))$, $$\Bigl|\mathbf E(rn,u+\tfrac rc)-\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2},\qquad \Bigl|\mathbf B(rn,u+\tfrac rc)-\frac{n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)}{c}\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}.$$

(c) (Retarded-time flux limit.) Let $\mathbf S:=\mu_0^{-1}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ and let $d\Omega$ be the surface measure on $S^2$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]). Then for every $u\in[t_0,T]$, $$\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}\bigl|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)\bigr|^2\,d\Omega(n).$$ This is a limit at fixed retarded time $u$, not at fixed observation time $t$; no decay or boundary condition at spatial infinity is assumed beyond the compact spatial support in (H1).
items.strategy:
Proof technique: direct, with explicit uniform estimates; the polar-coordinate identity uses the wave Cauchy problem as the definition of the retarded solution.

(a) On $\{|x|>2a\}$ one has $|x-y|\ge a>0$ for $y\in\overline B_a$, so the integrands of $\varphi$ and $\mathbf A$ are of class $C^\infty$ jointly in $(x,t,y)$ on a neighbourhood of $\{|x|>2a\}\times\mathbb R\times\overline B_a$; differentiating under the integral over the compact set $\overline B_a$ in each parameter direction ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]]) and using the chain rule for $(x,t)\mapsto(y,t-|x-y|/c)$ gives $\nabla_x[f(y,t-R/c)/R]=-\mathbf N[f/R^2+f_t/(cR)]$ and $\nabla_x\times[\mathbf J(y,t-R/c)/R]=-\mathbf N\times[\mathbf J/R^2+\mathbf J_t/(cR)]$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); substituting into $\mathbf E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$ gives the displayed field integrals and the smoothness claim. The identification with the wave Cauchy problem is the polar-coordinates identity: by [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], applied to $h=\mu_0c^2\rho$ and to each component $h=\mu_0J_k$ (to the positive and negative parts, then subtracted), $$\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy=\int_0^\infty r\,M_rh(x,t-r/c)\,dr,\qquad M_rh(x,v)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}h(x+rn,v)\,d\sigma(n);$$ substituting $r=c(t-v)$ in the $r$-integral with the one-dimensional $L^1$ change-of-variables formula for the $C^1$ diffeomorphism $v\mapsto c(t-v)$ ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]], applied on the compact interval where the continuous integrand is bounded) turns the right-hand side into $c^2\int_{t_0}^t(t-v)M_{c(t-v)}h(\cdot,v)(x)\,dv$ for $t\in[t_0,T]$, which is exactly the function displayed in clause (a) of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]] for zero Cauchy data at $t_0$ and source $h$.

(b) Elementary bounds in the Euclidean norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]): for $|y|\le a$ and $r\ge2a$ one has $R^2-(r-n\cdot y)^2=|y|^2-(n\cdot y)^2$ with $R+(r-n\cdot y)\ge r$, hence $|R-(r-n\cdot y)|\le a^2/r$, $|\mathbf N-n|\le(a+a^2/r)/(r-a)\le5a/r$ and $|1/R-1/r|\le(a+a^2/r)/(r(r-a))\le2a/r^2$, uniformly in $n,y$. Consequently $t-R/c=u+n\cdot y/c+O(a^2/(rc))$ uniformly, and comparing the field integrals of (a) with the candidate leading terms, each correction term (the $\rho/R^2$-term, the $\mathbf N-n$, $1/R-1/r$ and retarded-argument corrections) is bounded by an explicit constant times $r^{-2}$, the constants involving only $a,c,\mu_0$ and the suprema of $|\rho|,|\rho_t|,|\rho_{tt}|,|\mathbf J|,|\mathbf J_t|,|\mathbf J_{tt}|$ on the compact set $\overline B_a\times[t_0,T]$ (mean value theorem in the time variable; [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). The surviving terms of order $r^{-1}$ are $\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}\bigl[c\,n\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy-\int_{B_a}\mathbf J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy\bigr]$, the second integral being $\mathbf V(n,u)$ and the first computed from the continuity equation: applying the divergence theorem for a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]], with $\Omega$ a ball of radius $R>a$ containing the spatial support, whose boundary flux vanishes because $\mathbf J$ vanishes off $B_a$) to $y\mapsto\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ gives $0=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\operatorname{div}_y[\mathbf J(\cdot,u+n\cdot y/c)]=\int_{\mathbb R^3}[\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J+\frac nc\cdot\mathbf J_t](y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]); by (H2) and continuity of $\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J$, this is $\int\rho_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)dy=\frac1c n\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$. Substituting, $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}[c\,n\,\frac1c(n\cdot\mathbf V)-\mathbf V]=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}[n(n\cdot\mathbf V)-\mathbf V]=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times\mathbf V)$ by the vector triple-product identity, and the leading term of $\mathbf B$ is $-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi cr}n\times\mathbf V=\frac{n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}}{c}$, so the stated uniform errors follow with the constants just described.

(c) From the leading fields, $n\cdot\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}=0$ and $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{lead}}=\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}\times(n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})/c=(|E_{\mathrm{lead}}|^2n-(n\cdot\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})/c=|E_{\mathrm{lead}}|^2n/c$, while $|\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}|=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}|n\times(n\times\mathbf V)|=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}|n\times\mathbf V|$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Hence $r^2n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,u+r/c)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2+R(n,u,r)$ with $|R|\le C/r$ uniformly in $n,u$ for an explicit $C$ obtained from $\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$. The sphere is compact of finite surface measure, the map $n\mapsto|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2$ is continuous ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]] gives smoothness of $\mathbf I$, hence of $\mathbf V$, in $n$), and uniform convergence of the integrands gives the displayed limit without any further limit/integration exchange ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention used by that definition is declared in the item contract, [[def-countable-choice]]).
 Scalar normalization check for (a): phi=mu0 c²/(4pi) integral rho(y,t-R/c)/R, so -grad phi=mu0/(4pi) integral [c²N rho/R²+c N rho_t/R]; subtracting A_t adds -mu0 J_t/(4pi R). The second electric term has one factor c, consistent with (b)'s c n integral rho_t and epsilon0^-1=mu0 c².

items.proof:
**Proof technique:** direct; part (a) differentiates the retarded integrals and identifies them with the wave Cauchy solution, part (b) expands the field integrals uniformly in the far zone and derives the continuity identity, part (c) passes to the surface integral.

1.1 Smoothness of the potentials: for $x\in U$ and $y\in\overline B_a$ one has $R=|x-y|\ge|x|-a>0$, so the maps $(x,t,y)\mapsto\rho(y,t-R/c)/R$ and $(x,t,y)\mapsto\mathbf J(y,t-R/c)/R$ are $C^\infty$ on a neighbourhood of $U\times\mathbb R\times\overline B_a$ by [F6] and [F7]. Apply [F5] to the fixed compact set $K=\overline B_a$ once for each parameter direction with its one real parameter renamed to $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$ and $t$ (the remaining variables held fixed) and iterate on the resulting integrals: every differentiated integrand is again continuous on a neighbourhood of $K$, so each application is covered by the lemma and $\varphi$ and each component of $\mathbf A$ have continuous partial derivatives of every order on $U\times\mathbb R$, these differentiated parameter integrals are jointly continuous: on each compact parameter neighbourhood the continuous differentiated integrands are uniformly continuous on its product with $K$, so the integral of their difference is bounded by $\lambda(K)$ times their uniformly vanishing difference [F2]. Hence the potentials are $C^\infty$ on $U\times\mathbb R$ by [F7], so the derivatives defining the fields are ordinary derivatives even at $|x|=2a$. [F5, F6, F7, F3]

1.2 Elementary estimates in the far zone: for $y\in B_a$, $r\ge2a$ and $n\in S^2$, expanding $R^2=(r-\sigma)^2+|y|^2-\sigma^2$ with $\sigma=n\cdot y$ gives $|R-(r-\sigma)|=\bigl||y|^2-\sigma^2\bigr|/(R+r-\sigma)\le a^2/r$ because $R+r-\sigma\ge r-\sigma+|r-\sigma|\ge r$; consequently $|r-R|\le a+a^2/r$, $|\mathbf N-n|=|(r-R)n-y|/R\le(a+a^2/r+a)/(r-a)\le5a/r$, $|1/R-1/r|\le(a+a^2/r)/(r(r-a))\le3a/r^2$, and $|\delta_y|\le a^2/(rc)$, all uniformly in $y,n$. [F12, F1]

2.1 Field formulas: by [F6], $\nabla_xR=\mathbf N$, $\nabla_x(t-R/c)=-\mathbf N/c$ and $\nabla_x\times[\mathbf J(y,t-R/c)]=-\mathbf N\times\mathbf J_t(y,t-R/c)/c$, while $\nabla_x(1/R)=-\mathbf N/R^2$; hence $\nabla_x[\rho(y,t-R/c)/R]=-\mathbf N[\rho/R^2+\rho_t/(cR)]$ and $\nabla_x\times[\mathbf J(y,t-R/c)/R]=-\mathbf N\times[\mathbf J/R^2+\mathbf J_t/(cR)]$. Each of these first derivatives of the integrands is continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline B_a$, so by [F5] the derivatives may be taken under the integral: $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf A$ are given on $U$, in particular for $|x|\ge2a$, by the two displayed zero-extended integrals of the statement, since $\mathbf E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_t\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$. [step 1.1, F5, F6, F12]

2.2 Polar-coordinates identity: fix $x\in U$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, and let $h$ be either $\rho$ or one component $J_k$; then $y\mapsto h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/|x-y|$ vanishes off $\overline B_a$ and $|x-y|\ge|x|-a>0$ there, so the quotient on $\overline B_a$, extended by zero elsewhere, defines a bounded compactly supported Borel function $f$ on all of $\mathbb R^3$. The translation $T(z):=x+z$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\det DT=1$, so [F14] applied to the positive and negative parts of $f$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(x+z)\,dz$; applying [F9] to the positive and negative parts of $z\mapsto f(x+z)$, which at $z=\rho\omega$ equals $h(x+\rho\omega,t-\rho/c)/\rho$ and therefore has inner angular integral $\frac1\rho\int_{S^2}h(x+\rho n,t-\rho/c)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{4\pi}{\rho}M_\rho h(x,t-\rho/c)$, gives $\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{h(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}dy=\int_0^\infty r\,M_rh(x,t-r/c)\,dr$ with $M_rh(x,v)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}h(x+rn,v)\,d\Omega(n)$, because the inner angular integral is $4\pi M_rh$ and the radial factor is $r^2/r=r$. [step 1.1, F9, F14, F1, F3]

2.3 Continuity identity: fix $n,u$ and let $\rho_0>a$; the map $F(y):=\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)$ is $C^1$ on $\overline B_{\rho_0}$, and [F6] gives $\operatorname{div}F(y)=\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J(y,v_y)+\frac nc\cdot\mathbf J_t(y,v_y)$ with $v_y=u+n\cdot y/c$. By [F11] on $B_{\rho_0}$, whose boundary flux vanishes because $\mathbf J=0$ for $|y|>a$, $\int_{B_{\rho_0}}\operatorname{div}F\,dy=0$; substituting the chain-rule expression and using (H2), $0=\int_{B_{\rho_0}}\bigl[-\rho_t(y,v_y)+\frac1cn\cdot\mathbf J_t(y,v_y)\bigr]dy$. The integrands vanish for $|y|>a$ by (H1), so [F2] lets the integrals be taken over $B_a$; the second is $\frac1cn\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$ by the definition of $\mathbf V$, whence $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,v_y)\,dy=\frac1cn\cdot\mathbf V(n,u)$. [step 1.2, F11, F6, F2]

3.1 Identification with the Cauchy solution: fix $x\in U$. For $t>t_0$ the radial integrand of step 2.2 vanishes when $r>c(t-t_0)$, because then its source time is less than $t_0$. Apply [F10] to the affine diffeomorphism $v\mapsto c(t-v)$ from $(t_0,t)$ onto $(0,c(t-t_0))$, with absolute derivative $c$; the integrand is bounded on this finite interval, hence integrable. Endpoint values do not affect the Lebesgue integrals, and this gives $\int_0^\infty rM_rh(x,t-r/c)\,dr=c^2\int_{t_0}^t(t-v)M_{c(t-v)}h(x,v)\,dv$. At $t=t_0$ both sides are zero by (H1), so the identity holds throughout $[t_0,T]$. Multiplying it by $\mu_0c^2$ for $h=\rho$, and by $\mu_0$ for $h=J_k$, identifies $\varphi$ and $A_k$ respectively with the zero-data Cauchy solutions of [F8] with sources $\mu_0c^2\rho$ and $\mu_0J_k$. This holds on $U\times[t_0,T]$ and in particular at $|x|=2a$. [step 2.2, F10, F8, F1]

3.2 Uniform error estimates: fix $n,u,r$, let $\mathrm{ret}$ denote the argument $v_y+\delta_y$ and $0$ the argument $v_y$, and write $F_{\mathrm{tot}}:=c^2\mathbf N\rho_{\mathrm{ret}}/R^2+c\mathbf N\rho_{t,\mathrm{ret}}/R-\mathbf J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}/R$ and $F_{\mathrm{lead}}:=\frac1r\bigl(c\,n\,\rho_{t,0}-\mathbf J_{t,0}\bigr)$, so that the field formula of step 2.1 and the definition of $\mathbf V$ give $\mathbf E(rn,u+r/c)-\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{B_a}(F_{\mathrm{tot}}-F_{\mathrm{lead}})\,dy$ by the linearity of the integral. Every source factor is bounded by its supremum on $\overline B_a\times[t_0,T]$, and (H1) makes $\rho$ and $\mathbf J$ vanish on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times((-\infty,t_0)\cup(T,\infty))$, hence makes all their partial derivatives vanish there too, so these suprema also dominate the retarded arguments $v_y+\delta_y$; the mean value theorem [F4] gives $|\rho_{t,\mathrm{ret}}-\rho_{t,0}|\le\Gamma_{\rho tt}|\delta_y|$ and $|\mathbf J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}-\mathbf J_{t,0}|\le\Gamma_{Jtt}|\delta_y|$: when the difference is nonzero, apply [F4] to its scalar projection onto the unit direction of that difference, and use Cauchy-Schwarz from [F12], and using $R^{-1}\le2/r$, $R^{-2}\le4/r^2$ and $|\mathbf N/R-n/r|\le|\mathbf N-n|/R+|1/R-1/r|\le13a/r^2$ yields $|F_{\mathrm{tot}}-F_{\mathrm{lead}}|\le\Gamma_E'/r^2$, with $\Gamma_E':=4c^2\Gamma_\rho+13ca\Gamma_{\rho t}+a^2\Gamma_{\rho tt}+3a\Gamma_{Jt}+a^2\Gamma_{Jtt}/c$ for all $r\ge2a$; hence, by the triangle inequality for the integral and the finiteness of $\lambda(B_a)$, $\bigl|\mathbf E(rn,u+r/c)-\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)\bigr|\le\Gamma_E/r^2$ with $\Gamma_E:=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\Gamma_E'\lambda(B_a)$. The same computation applied to $\mathbf B(rn,u+r/c)=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{B_a}\mathbf N\times[\mathbf J_{\mathrm{ret}}/R^2+\mathbf J_{t,\mathrm{ret}}/(cR)]dy$ and to $n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}/c=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{B_a}\frac1{cr}n\times\mathbf J_{t,0}\,dy$ gives $\bigl|\mathbf B(rn,u+r/c)-n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)/c\bigr|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$, for $\Gamma_B:=\frac{\mu_0\lambda(B_a)}{4\pi}(4\Gamma_J+13a\Gamma_{Jt}/c+a^2\Gamma_{Jtt}/c^2)$. [step 1.2, step 2.3, F2, F3, F4, F12]

4.1 Smoothness of the far-zone moments: the map $(n,u)\mapsto\mathbf I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ and its partial derivative $\partial_u\mathbf I=\int_{B_a}\mathbf J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy=\mathbf V(n,u)$ are $C^\infty$ in $(n,u)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: apply [F5] repeatedly in the directions $n_1,n_2,n_3,u$ with the fixed compact set $\overline B_a$, each differentiated integrand again being continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline B_a$; the integrals over $B_a$ and $\overline B_a$ agree because the smooth sources and all their derivatives vanish on $|y|=a$ by continuity from $|y|>a$. In particular $n\mapsto|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2$ is continuous for each fixed $u$. [step 3.2, F5, F6, F7, F12]

4.2 Pointwise flux asymptotics: by step 3.2 write $\mathbf E=\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}+\boldsymbol\rho_E$ and $\mathbf B=n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}/c+\boldsymbol\rho_B$ at $(rn,u+r/c)$ with $|\boldsymbol\rho_E|\le\Gamma_E/r^2$, $|\boldsymbol\rho_B|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$; then $n\cdot\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}=0$ and $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}\times(n\times\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}})=|\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}|^2n$ by [F12], while $|\mathbf E_{\mathrm{lead}}|=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|$ because $|n\times(n\times\mathbf V)|=|n\times\mathbf V|$. Expanding the cross product bilinearly, the error terms are $O(r^{-3})$, so $r^2n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,u+r/c)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2+R(n,u,r)$ with $|R(n,u,r)|\le C/r$ for a constant $C$ depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and the source suprema, uniformly in $n\in S^2$ and $u\in[t_0,T]$. [step 3.2, F12, F2]

5.1 Flux limit: by [F13] the surface integral over the compact sphere of a bounded Borel function is finite and monotone, so for every $u\in[t_0,T]$ and $r\ge2a$ the difference $\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,u+r/c)\,d\Omega(n)-\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2\,d\Omega(n)=\int_{S^2}R(n,u,r)\,d\Omega(n)$ has absolute value at most $\frac{C}{r}\int_{S^2}1\,d\Omega$, which tends to $0$; the function $n\mapsto|n\times\mathbf V(n,u)|^2$ is continuous by step 4.1, so its surface integral is the displayed finite constant. Hence the stated limit at fixed retarded time $u$ follows; no step compares different values of $u$, so the limit is asserted only at fixed retarded time. [step 4.2, step 4.1, F13, F2] ∎

title: Em Causal Response And Radiation Prerequisites — Examples

items.title: Hypothesis boundaries: a causal response without passivity, and the fixed-retarded-time flux limit
items.reference: mathematical-example-verifications.md#ex-em-causal-response-and-radiation-prerequisites-hypothesis-boundaries; clause (ii) added by this scaffolder to exercise the second theorem's declared dependency (recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the surface-integral conventions used by [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]].

(i) (Causality without passivity.) In this clause also assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]), inherited from the exact AC supplier. Let $K(s):=-e^{-s}$ for $s\ge0$. Then $K$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and $sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ (indeed $K'=e^{-s}=-K$, $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=1$ and $\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$), so the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] applies: $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)ds$ is a bounded causal linear response on bounded continuous histories, its transfer function is $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and its boundary value $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ satisfies $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ for every $\omega>0$. Hence the Hermitian dissipative part $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$ is strictly negative, not positive semidefinite, and the monochromatic period-averaged work of clause (d) of that theorem is strictly negative for $d=1$, every $e\ne0$ and every $\omega>0$ (with any response normalization $\varepsilon_0>0$), although the response is causal and its entry satisfies the dispersion relations of clause (c). Nonnegative period-averaged work (passivity) is therefore an additional condition on the model, not a consequence of temporal causality.

(ii) (The flux limit needs fixed retarded time.) In the setting of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]], fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and $n\in S^2$, and let $r>\max\{2a,\;a+c(t-t_0)\}$. Then for every $y\in B_a$ one has $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$, so $t-R/c<t_0$; by hypothesis (H1) of that theorem the functions $\rho,\rho_t,\mathbf J,\mathbf J_t$ all vanish at $(y,t-R/c)$, so every integrand in the field formulas of clause (a) of that theorem vanishes and $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$, hence $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. Therefore $\int_{S^2}r^2\,n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)\,d\Omega(n)=0$ for all such $r$: at fixed observation time the far-zone flux integral is identically zero beyond the light cone of the compact spacetime support, whereas clause (c) of that theorem is a limit at fixed retarded time. These limits may agree for a particular source, including the zero source. They cannot be interchanged as a general theorem: the conserved smooth sources constructed below have a strictly positive fixed-retarded-time flux limit.
items.strategy:
Proof technique: direct computation and direct substitution into the two cited theorems.

(i) The real exponential is differentiable with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]) and $\exp(-s)>0$ with $\exp(-s)=1/\exp(s)$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]), so $s\mapsto K(s)=-e^{-s}$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K'=e^{-s}=-K$ ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). For every $N>0$ the Newton-Leibniz formula gives $\int_0^Ne^{-s}ds=1-e^{-N}$ and integration by parts (with $u=s$, $v=-e^{-s}$) gives $\int_0^Nse^{-s}ds=1-(1+N)e^{-N}$ ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], [[thm-integration-by-parts]]); the continuous real integrands have the same Lebesgue integrals by [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]]; [[thm-c1-lipschitz-ac-bv-hierarchy]] proves the explicit $C^1$ kernel is absolutely continuous on each compact interval in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]; the displayed Newton-Leibniz integral representations agree with the Lebesgue FTC under this regularity. Thus it has the absolute-continuity property required by the integrable branch of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]], and passing to the limit with monotone convergence for the nonnegative integrands gives $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$, so $K,K',sK(s)\in L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). Clause (a) of the theorem therefore gives the bounded causal response. For the transfer function, fix real $\omega$; the complex exponential is entire with derivative itself and the complex chain rule gives that $s\mapsto F(s)=\exp((-1+i\omega)s)/(-1+i\omega)$ is a primitive of $s\mapsto\exp((-1+i\omega)s)$ on $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]], [[def-complex-exponential]]), so the fundamental theorem for complex line integrals along the interval path $[0,N]\ni s\mapsto s$ gives $\int_{[0,N]}\exp((-1+i\omega)s)\,ds=F(N)-F(0)$ ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-for-complex-line-integrals]], [[def-complex-primitive]], [[def-complex-line-integral-over-a-rectifiable-path]], [[thm-riemann-stieltjes-and-parametric-contour-integrals-agree]]). Hence $\int_0^N(-e^{-s})e^{i\omega s}ds=-(F(N)-F(0))$, and $\left|e^{(-1+i\omega)N}\right|=e^{-N}\to0$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]); letting $N\to\infty$ with dominated convergence for the integrands dominated by $e^{-s}$ gives $\chi(\omega)=-1/(1-i\omega)$, and the same computation with $z$ in place of $\omega$ gives $\chi(z)=-1/(1-iz)$ for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]). Taking real and imaginary parts ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) gives $\chi(\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ and $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ because $\omega>0$. With $d=1$, $e=1$ and $\varepsilon_0>0$, clause (d) of the theorem gives period-averaged work $\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)<0$ and $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)<0$, so the passivity condition fails while causality holds: this witnesses the logical independence recorded in the theorem's proof discussion.

(ii) For $y\in B_a$ the reverse triangle inequality gives $R=|rn-y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), hence $t-R/c<t_0$ and all four source functions vanish at the arguments appearing in the field integrals of clause (a) of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]]; each integrand is identically zero on $B_a$, so $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$ and therefore $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=\mu_0^{-1}n\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$. The surface integral of the zero function vanishes ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), so the fixed-observation-time flux integral is $0$ for every $r>\max\{2a,a+c(t-t_0)\}$, while the limit displayed in clause (c) of that theorem is taken with $u$ fixed and $r\to\infty$ along $t=u+r/c$; the two formulations therefore differ and the retarded-time one is essential.

items.proof:
**Proof technique:** direct computation for clause (i); direct substitution into the cited theorem and the triangle inequality for clause (ii).

1.1 The kernel $K(s)=-e^{-s}$ is of class $C^1$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $K'=e^{-s}=-K$ by [F1] and [F6]; $K(s)<0$ for every $s$, and $|K(s)|=e^{-s}$, $|K'(s)|=e^{-s}$, $|sK(s)|=se^{-s}$. Newton–Leibniz gives $\int_0^Ne^{-s}ds=1-e^{-N}$ and integration by parts gives $\int_0^Nse^{-s}ds=1-(1+N)e^{-N}$ for every $N$, and [F2] converts these to Lebesgue integrals; for $N>0$ the nonnegative exponential series gives $e^N\ge N^2/2$ by [F1], so $e^{-N}\to0$ and $Ne^{-N}\le2/N\to0$; since the integrands are nonnegative, [F3] lets $N\to\infty$, giving $\int_0^\infty e^{-s}ds=1$ and $\int_0^\infty se^{-s}ds=1$. Hence $K,K',sK\in L^1(0,\infty)$ and, by [F5], $K$ is locally absolutely continuous on $[0,\infty)$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6]

1.2 A conserved smooth source with nonzero radiation. For the constants of clause (ii), put $u_*:=(t_0+T)/2$, $b:=(T-t_0)/8$ and $\epsilon:=\min(a/2,bc/2)>0$. By [F13] choose $\psi:\mathbb R^3\to[0,1]$ smooth, equal to $1$ on $\overline B_{\epsilon/2}$ and supported in $B_\epsilon$, and $\theta:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ smooth, equal to $1$ on $[-b,b]$ and supported in $(-2b,2b)$. Define $f(v):=(v-u_*)^2\theta(v-u_*)$, $\rho(y,v):=-\partial_3\psi(y)f(v)$ and $\mathbf J(y,v):=(0,0,\psi(y)f'(v))$. These functions are smooth by [F13], their spatial support is contained in $B_\epsilon\subset B_a$, and their temporal support is contained in $(u_*-2b,u_*+2b)\subset(t_0,T)$, so (H1) holds. Direct coordinate differentiation gives $\rho_t=-\partial_3\psi\,f'$ and $\operatorname{div}_y\mathbf J=\partial_3\psi\,f'$, proving (H2). By [F14] and monotonicity, $C_\psi:=\int_{B_a}\psi(y)\,dy$ satisfies $0<\lambda(B_{\epsilon/2})\le C_\psi\le\lambda(B_\epsilon)<\infty$. [F13, F14, F6, F4, construct]

2.1 Therefore the integrable branch of clause (c) of [F9] applies to $K$: $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)ds$ is a bounded causal linear response on bounded continuous histories by clause (a), $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}ds$ is well defined and holomorphic on $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, continuous on the closed upper half-plane, and its boundary values satisfy the dispersion relations of clause (c). [step 1.1, F9, F4]

2.2 Positive fixed-retarded-time flux. If $y\in\operatorname{supp}\psi$ and $n\in S^2$, then $|n\cdot y|/c\le|y|/c<\epsilon/c\le b/2$, so $\theta=1$ near $u_*+n\cdot y/c-u_*$ and $f''(u_*+n\cdot y/c)=2$. Thus $\mathbf V(n,u_*)=2C_\psi p$ for every $n$, where $p:=(0,0,1)$. Orthogonal invariance in [F14] makes the three integrals $\int_{S^2}n_j^2\,d\Omega$ equal; their sum is $\int_{S^2}|n|^2\,d\Omega=4\pi$, so each is $4\pi/3$. The cross-product coordinates give $|n\times p|^2=n_1^2+n_2^2=1-n_3^2$, hence $\int_{S^2}|n\times p|^2\,d\Omega=8\pi/3$. Clause (c) of [F10] now gives the fixed-retarded-time limit $\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\,4C_\psi^2\,\frac{8\pi}{3}=\frac{2\mu_0C_\psi^2}{3\pi c}>0$. [step 1.2, F10, F11, F14, algebra]

3.1 Computation of the transfer function: fix $z$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ and put $\lambda:=iz-1$, so $\lambda\ne0$ and $|e^{\lambda N}|=e^{-N}e^{-N\operatorname{Im}z}\le e^{-N}\to0$ by [F8]. For every $N>0$ the function $s\mapsto e^{\lambda s}$ is continuous, so its Lebesgue integral over $(0,N)$ agrees with its Riemann and parametric line integral over $[0,N]$ by [F2] and [F7], and the first fundamental theorem of [F7] applied to the primitive $F(s)=e^{\lambda s}/\lambda$ gives $\int_0^Ne^{\lambda s}ds=(e^{\lambda N}-1)/\lambda$; the truncated integrands $s\mapsto-e^{\lambda s}\mathbf 1_{(0,N)}(s)$ converge pointwise to $s\mapsto-e^{\lambda s}$ and are dominated by $e^{-s}\in L^1(0,\infty)$, so [F4] gives $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty(-e^{\lambda s})ds=-\lim_{N\to\infty}(e^{\lambda N}-1)/\lambda=1/\lambda=-1/(1-iz)$, where for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$ the first equality is the defining integral of clause (c) of [F9] and for real $z$ it is its continuous boundary value. [step 2.1, F7, F8, F4, F2]

4.1 Boundary values and the dissipative part: for real $\omega$, step 3.1 gives $\chi(\omega)=-1/(1-i\omega)=-(1+i\omega)/(1+\omega^2)$ by multiplication with the conjugate denominator, so $\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=-\omega/(1+\omega^2)<0$ for every $\omega>0$; for $d=1$ and $e\ne0$, $e^*\chi(\omega)e=|e|^2\chi(\omega)$ and $e^*M(\omega)e=|e|^2\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)<0$, so the Hermitian dissipative part $M(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$ is strictly negative and in particular not positive semidefinite. By clause (d) of [F9] the monochromatic period-averaged work equals $(\varepsilon_0\omega/2)|e|^2\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)$, which is strictly negative for every $e\ne0$ and every $\varepsilon_0>0$, while steps 2.1 and 3.1 exhibit the response as causal with dispersion relations. Passivity is therefore an additional condition and not a consequence of causality. [step 3.1, F9, F8, F4]

5.1 Clause (ii): fix $t\in\mathbb R$, $n\in S^2$ and $r>\max\{2a,a+c(t-t_0)\}$, so $r>2a$ and $r-a>c(t-t_0)$. For every $y\in B_a$ the triangle inequality of [F11] gives $R=|rn-y|\ge r-|y|\ge r-a>c(t-t_0)$, hence $t-R/c<t_0$; since (H1) makes $\rho$ and $\mathbf J$ vanish on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times((-\infty,t_0)\cup(T,\infty))$, all their partial derivatives vanish there too, so $\rho,\rho_t,\mathbf J,\mathbf J_t$ all vanish at $(y,t-R/c)$ for every $y\in B_a$, and the integrands of the field formulas of clause (a) of [F10] vanish pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$. Hence $\mathbf E(rn,t)=\mathbf B(rn,t)=0$, so $n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)=\mu_0^{-1}n\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)(rn,t)=0$ for every $n\in S^2$, and [F12] gives $\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot\mathbf S(rn,t)\,d\Omega(n)=0$ for all such $r$. [step 4.1, F10, F11, F12]

6.1 For every admissible source, step 5.1 gives an eventually zero flux integral at fixed observation time. For the admissible source of step 1.2, step 2.2 gives a strictly positive limit along $t=u_*+r/c$. Consequently a fixed-observation-time limit cannot replace the fixed-retarded-time limit as a theorem about all these sources; zero or nonradiating sources may give zero in both limits.
